findings.citation: When debugging Kotlin code, IntelliJ IDEA allows you to suspend the execution and diagnose problems that the code in coroutines may have. The debug information is available even if the coroutine is not running at the moment.
findings.claim: IntelliJ IDEA's debugger provides a dedicated Coroutines tab showing running/suspended coroutine status, full Variables tab functionality, watches, expression evaluation, and thread dumps that include Kotlin coroutines.

findings.citation: IntelliJ IDEA's thread dump includes Java platform threads, virtual threads, and Kotlin coroutines.
findings.claim: IntelliJ IDEA's thread dump feature explicitly covers Kotlin coroutines alongside platform and virtual threads.

findings.citation: The Debug Tool Window now contains a new Coroutines tab. It is visible by default, and you can switch it on and off
findings.claim: The dedicated Coroutines debugger tab was introduced as a first-party Kotlin plugin feature (Kotlin 1.4), showing both running and suspended coroutines.

findings.citation: One common issue is that variables used before calling a suspend function may be optimized out, making their values unavailable in the debugger.
findings.claim: A known limitation exists: variables used before a suspend call can be optimized out and become invisible in the debugger unless a special compiler flag is enabled, which is not recommended for production use.

findings.citation: It's a little soul-crushing that Android Studio doesn't offer the awesome GUI option above.
findings.claim: Community reporting notes the polished GUI coroutine-debugging experience is available in IntelliJ IDEA but Android Studio lacks the same GUI option.

findings.citation: Kotlin runs on the JVM, which means you get access to the entire ecosystem of JVM profiling tools. But Kotlin also has its own idioms, like coroutines, extension functions, and inline functions, that can behave differently than what you might expect when profiling.
findings.claim: Kotlin, running on the JVM, has access to the entire mature JVM profiling tool ecosystem, though Kotlin-specific idioms like coroutines and inline functions require special interpretation of profiler output.

findings.citation: Java Flight Recorder (JFR) is built into the JDK since Java 11 and has low overhead in production. It collects CPU samples, memory allocation data, garbage collection events, thread activity, and I/O operations.
findings.claim: Java Flight Recorder, built into the JDK since Java 11, provides low-overhead production profiling of CPU, memory allocation, GC, thread activity and I/O, and is recommended as the first tool for Kotlin profiling.

findings.citation: async-profiler—a low-overhead sampling profiler designed specifically for Java and other JVM languages (Kotlin, Scala, etc.)
findings.claim: async-profiler is a widely used low-overhead sampling profiler explicitly supporting Kotlin (and other JVM languages), producing flame graphs, HTML reports, and JFR output, and is safe for production use.

findings.citation: YourKit is a commercial, GUI-based Java and .NET profiler that provides deep insight into application behavior. It has CPU and memory profiling, heap dump analysis, thread and deadlock detection, allocation tracking features.
findings.claim: YourKit is an actively maintained (2026 release cadence) commercial GUI profiler offering CPU/memory profiling, heap dump analysis, thread/deadlock detection, and allocation tracking for JVM languages including Kotlin.

findings.citation: Introduced in Android Studio 3.0, the Android Profiler provides a way to monitor CPU, networking and memory metrics of an app in realtime as it is running on a device or emulator.
findings.claim: For Android Kotlin apps, Android Studio ships a dedicated built-in Profiler covering real-time CPU, networking, and memory metrics.

findings.citation: To record Java/Kotlin allocations, select the Track Memory Consumption (Java/Kotlin Allocations) task from the profiler Home tab.
findings.claim: The Android Studio Profiler explicitly supports recording Java/Kotlin object allocations for memory analysis, including sampled vs. full allocation tracking modes.

metric.debugger_profiler_support.limitations: Profiler/debugger maturity is largely inherited from the shared JVM/Android platform ecosystem rather than being Kotlin-specific tooling; this is consistent with Kotlin's design as a JVM-hosted language and is scored as accumulated ecosystem maturity per the metric definition, distinct from language-level debuggability scored under Language Quality.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.measurement: Kotlin inherits the full mature JVM debugger/profiler stack (IntelliJ debugger, JFR, async-profiler, YourKit, JProfiler, VisualVM) plus a dedicated first-party Coroutines debugger tab and Android Studio's dedicated CPU/Memory/Network/Energy profiler, with one documented rough edge around suspend-function variable visibility.

bands: 90-100: Mature, deeply integrated first-party debugger with native support for the language's concurrency/async model, plus multiple robust, actively maintained profilers (CPU/memory/allocation) with low-overhead production-safe options.

75-89: Solid first-party debugger with most standard features and dedicated tooling for the language's concurrency model, with some known rough edges (e.g., optimized-out state in async code), backed by a mature, shared platform profiler ecosystem.
50-74: Basic debugger functions but concurrency/async debugging is weak or unsupported; profiler tooling exists but is limited or third-party only.
25-49: Debugging is possible but crude (e.g., print-based only) with no meaningful profiler ecosystem.
0-24: No meaningful debugger or profiler tooling.

findings.citation: JetBrains provides official Kotlin support for the following IDEs and code editors: IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio. You can also install the official Kotlin by JetBrains extension for Visual Studio Code, which is currently in Alpha. Other IDEs and code editors only have Kotlin community-supported plugins.
findings.claim: JetBrains provides official IDE support for three environments: IntelliJ IDEA, Android Studio, and VS Code (currently in Alpha); everything else is community-supported.

findings.citation: IntelliJ IDEA is an IDE designed for JVM languages, such as Kotlin and Java, to maximize developer productivity. It does the routine and repetitive tasks for you by providing clever code completion, static code analysis, and refactorings.
findings.claim: IntelliJ IDEA is purpose-built for JVM languages (Kotlin/Java) with clever code completion, static analysis, and refactorings, and the Kotlin plugin ships bundled with every release.

findings.citation: Android Studio is the official IDE for Android app development, based on IntelliJ IDEA. On top of IntelliJ's powerful code editor and developer tools, Android Studio offers even more features that enhance your productivity when building Android apps.
findings.claim: Android Studio is the official Google IDE for Android, built on IntelliJ IDEA, with the Kotlin plugin bundled in every release.

findings.citation: Today at KotlinConf 2026, we announced the Alpha release of the official Kotlin extension for Visual Studio Code. IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio remain the most complete environments for Kotlin development.
findings.claim: At KotlinConf 2026, JetBrains announced the Alpha release of an official Kotlin extension for VS Code, built on the same code-insight infrastructure as the IntelliJ Kotlin plugin, but IntelliJ/Android Studio remain the most complete environments.

findings.citation: The Kotlin by JetBrains extension connects VS Code to the Kotlin Language Server built on IntelliJ IDEA's code-insight infrastructure and the Kotlin plugin implementation.
findings.claim: The VS Code extension is powered by the same Kotlin Language Server built on IntelliJ IDEA's code-insight infrastructure, and its Alpha feature set covers completion, diagnostics, navigation, quick-fixes, formatting, and project import.

findings.citation: IntelliJ IDEA provides full Kotlin Multiplatform support. Android Studio is another stable solution for Kotlin Multiplatform.
findings.claim: IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio provide full Kotlin Multiplatform support including a dedicated KMP IDE plugin with debugging capabilities for iOS apps and Compose Multiplatform tooling.

findings.citation: Android Studio dominates native Android work because Google ships it and writes Kotlin as the official Android language.
findings.claim: Industry commentary independently confirms IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio as the dominant, most complete Kotlin/Android tooling pair in 2026, with VS Code strong only for cross-platform (Flutter/RN) stacks rather than native Kotlin.

metric.ide_editor_support_quality.limitations: Popularity/usage percentages cited in secondary sources (e.g., developer-preference percentages) are self-reported survey figures from third-party blogs and are used only as contextual color, not as the scoring basis.
metric.ide_editor_support_quality.measurement: Kotlin has two deeply mature, first-party JetBrains/Google IDEs (IntelliJ IDEA and Android Studio) built on the same platform, plus an official (Alpha-stage) VS Code extension sharing the same code-insight core, with all other editors reduced to community-supported plugins/LSP.

bands: 90-100: Multiple full-featured first-party/official IDEs with deep semantic completion, refactoring, navigation, plus official support (even if early-stage) in a mainstream general-purpose editor, backed by a shared language-server/code-insight core.

75-89: One deeply mature flagship IDE with full features plus official but less complete support in at least one other major editor, OR full support in 2+ IDEs but only community (non-official) support elsewhere.
50-74: Adequate LSP-based completion/navigation across editors but no standout first-party flagship IDE experience, or a flagship IDE with only unofficial/community plugins elsewhere.
25-49: Basic syntax highlighting/completion only in most editors; immature or unmaintained tooling.
0-24: Minimal or no meaningful IDE/editor tooling.
